by others, most earnestly demands of you, Princes, that by your generosity you thus join your efforts, so that through their support public peace and tranquility may be preserved. But there is no reason for me to add fuel to the fire for one who runs of his own accord, since among all the Princes of our Germany scarcely another may be found who loves, fosters, protects, and honors letters and those who are renowned for some reputation of learning as much as you do.

Moved, therefore, by the splendor of your nobility and the many other most excellent virtues that shine forth in you, I have dedicated to Your Highness these commentaries on the history of plants, which I have indeed adorned with much toil and expense. For I knew that they required not common, but some outstanding patronage, since scarcely any other treatise can be so exposed and open to the calumnies of many as that which is undertaken to explain the nature of plants. Accordingly, since I was led to the most certain hope that these our labors would find no ordinary favor among the candid and just from the inscription of your most illustrious name, and that for this reason the impudence of slanderous critics would be broken, I chose you indeed from among so great a number of distinguished Princes of character to whom I might most properly dedicate these very works. Therefore, when you receive them, most illustrious PRINCE, you will resolve that the defense and preservation of this part of medicine, which investigates the natures of plants, is commended to you. That you may eagerly and willingly take this upon yourself, I know many things will move you: but most especially this very fact, that scarcely from any other matter does the enduring presence and benevolence of God shine forth more than from so varied a form and nature of plants, while we consider that all these were established by God Himself for the use of man. If, therefore, anything else, the diligent contemplation of herbs certainly arouses, indeed confirms in our minds this most excellent opinion: that men are a care to God, who so anxiously labor in joining and protecting them, while they adorn the earth with so many most elegant and excellent plants, by which they may drive away so many diseases. The examples of your most excellent Kings and Princes, which we have recounted above, will also not a little encourage you to undertake this care. But most of all, the immense benefit that will come to all from the preservation of this part of medicine will urge you on. Finally, the wonderful delight that will come upon your spirit in contemplating so many kinds of herbs will move you to both the love and defense of herbal medicine. For what is more pleasant, what more delightful than to behold the plants which the most good and great God has painted with so many and such varied colors, has crowned with so many most elegant flowers, whose color no painter has ever been able sufficiently to express: and has adorned with so many seeds and fruits, the use of which is greatest both in the kitchen and in medicine. But there is no need for me to attempt to draw you further into admiration of this part of medicine, since you are already so held by its study and love that scarcely anything else delights you more. For never would you have expended so much effort and expense in constructing gardens with so many trees and herbs, if the delight of the matter and a singular love did not draw you to it. It now remains, most illustrious PRINCE, that in accordance with your excellent humanity, which is akin to your own likeness, you receive this our gift with a glad countenance, as a token and witness of my love and respect toward Your Highness, and that you honor me with your favor and defend me by your authority from the calumnies of the envious. Moreover, there is good hope that this garden which we present to Your Highness will be most welcome, not only because in it you may find most elegantly painted herbs of almost every kind, but also because from it you may gather remedies for all kinds of diseases. Acinus signifies not merely the inner seeds of a grape, as some think, but the whole fruit, consisting of juice, the part that is like flesh, the grape seeds, and the skin surrounding it externally. Galen is witness; in book 2 of On the Properties of Foods he writes: ‘The body of the acinus consists of four parts: namely, that which is like its flesh; the liquid dispersed through it, from which wine is made; the seed; and the membranous covering that encloses all these externally.’ Aculei are any rather hard structures tapered to a point that inflict a prick like little spikes. Acus is the chaff of grain, that is, the lightest part adhering to it, which winnowing fans throw beyond the threshing floor. Adnata, Adnascentia, or Appendices are the little branches that a stem sometimes sends out from itself, like new and additional offspring. They are so called because they seem to grow onto and be added to the stem. The Greeks call them paraphyades because they sprout and grow around the stem. Alae are the hollow angles between a stem and its branches, from which new growth emerges through the recess; their name is transferred from human armpits. The Greeks call them maschalas. Alabastra are small vessels made of very hard and cold material for preserving perfumes. The Greeks so named them because their smoothness made them difficult to grasp and hold in the hands, and they slipped away. Hence the stone alabastrites, now called alabaster, was named because alabastra were made from it. Aluta is skin or hide after it has been dressed for making shoes and other articles. p0043-r013.text: It has leaves of the ivy family, but much softer and rounder. Between the leaves at the root are purple, fragrant flowers resembling the calyx of henbane, within which is seed not unlike a berry. It has many jointed, slender, oblique roots, very like those of grass but much finer, fragrant, warming, and very biting to the tongue. Here, however, we thought it right to warn the reader that every copy of Dioscorides is corrupt at this passage: they wrongly read either πυκνότερα or μικρότερα, where μαλακώτερα should be written. This can be proved partly by Pliny’s testimony and partly by the judgment of the senses themselves. Pliny, in book xij, chapter xij, describes Asarum thus: ‘It has leaves like ivy, only rounder and softer.’ If anyone submits the matter to sensory judgment and compares Asarum with ivy, he will certainly find that Asarum’s leaves are neither denser nor smaller than ivy leaves, since Asarum’s leaves are much larger than ivy’s. Since ivy leaves are much smaller by comparison, it is perfectly clear that μαλακώτερα should be read in place of μικρότερα. Pliny and sensory judgment alike support this reading, as stated: to the touch, this plant’s leaves are much softer than ivy leaves. Further, the change from one word to the other is easy. For these reasons I have said that Asarum’s leaves are μαλακώτερα—that is, softer than ivy leaves—as indeed they are.

p0177-r017.text: Buphthalmum puts forth a tender stem, leaves like fennel, and yellow flowers larger than those of Anthemis, shaped like eyes, from which it takes its name. These features agree exactly with the herb that ordinary herbalists call Cotula non foetida: its stems are tender and its leaves like fennel. The heads in Coronopus, however, are much thinner and longer than in Psyllium, as the illustration will graphically show. From these observations, it is also evident that those are entirely mistaken who contend that prickly grass and Coronopus are one and the same herb, since they appear to differ considerably in form. I therefore could not depict them in their true colors and forms except by hearsay.
